amendments.rule: **A purpose `לְ` + infinitive construct recast as a finite clause gives the complementizer to the preposition and the supplied subject and modal to the infinitive.** The ASV writes *that men may bring*, *that I may be glorified*. This is rule 48's division outside the privative `מִן`, and for the same reason: the complementizer is what the preposition contributes, while a supplied subject pronoun and a separately written modal belong to the verb, as rule 17 keeps a subject pronoun with its verb. The corpus puts the *that* on the preposition in 28 units across 17 chapters and never on the infinitive, so this too is settled. Where the ASV writes no complementizer at all there is nothing to place, and the `לְ` goes `unrepresented` under rule 40. **A temporal preposition before an infinitive construct is read the same way.** Where `בְּ` or `כְּ` + infinitive is recast as a finite temporal clause — `בְּחֻמָּם` → *When they are heated*, `בְּלֶכְתּוֹ` → *when he went*, `כְּבֹאֲךָ` → *When thou comest*, `כְּכַלֹּתְךָ` → *when thou hast made an end* — the preposition takes the *when*, the infinitive keeps the verb, and the suffix takes the subject pronoun the ASV writes for it under rule 18. The corpus aligns `בְּ` to *when* in 45 units, so the temporal case is settled on the same footing as the purpose case. Read the preposition that is present rather than its lemma: a `לְ` heading such a phrase goes the same way even where its object is the noun rather than the infinitive, as in `לְקוֹל תִּתּוֹ` → *When he uttereth his voice*. **But only a preposition that still has an English word to take can take it.** Where no preposition is present and the construct relation itself is what the English *when* realizes, rule 19 puts that word on the *nomen rectum*, which is the infinitive: `עֵת הִדְרִיכָהּ` → *at the time when it is trodden* gives *at the time* to `עֵת` and *when ... is trodden* to the infinitive. **And a preposition on which the ASV has already spent its own English word is in the same position as an absent one.** Where the preposition heads a construct noun, the ASV writes a word for that preposition and a second temporal word besides, the second answers to the construct relation and not to the preposition, so rule 19 puts it on the *nomen rectum*: `בְּיוֹם הֵעָשׂוֹתוֹ` → *in the day when they shall make it* gives *in* to the `בְּ` and *the day* to `יוֹם`, leaving *when they shall make* to the infinitive, whose own suffix takes the pronoun rule 18 gives it. Count the ASV's function words against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s and rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s: a preposition holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, and giving it both would leave the construct's relation unrendered against rule 2.
amendments.why: Rule 52's closing sentence conditions the rectum reading on no preposition being present, which leaves EZK.43.18's `בְּיוֹם הֵעָשׂוֹתוֹ` → *in the day when they shall make it* undecided: a `בְּ` is present but has already been spent on *in*, so a literal reading would force the *when* onto it as a second word and leave the construct relation between `יוֹם` and its infinitive unrendered, against rule 2. The rule already reasons exactly this way for `עֵת הִדְרִיכָהּ`, where the same construct relation carries the *when*; the amendment widens the condition from an absent preposition to one whose own word is already written, and grounds the test in the counting rules 42 and 29 already use. The corpus rows supplied for `בְּ` do not contradict it — its 235 *when* units and 2775 *in* units are the cases where the ASV writes one word or the other, not both — and `בְּיוֹם` plus infinitive construct recurs widely enough across the OT that leaving the gap would be paid for by every chapter after this one. Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule so the over-broad sentence is corrected where it stands rather than cross-referenced.

conventions: בֶּן־בָּקָר after פַּר is one unit under rule 30, rendered by the single English word *young* and headed on בֶּן, which carries the sense the one word spends itself on; the indefinite *a* goes to פַּר under rule 15 and the unit is discontinuous around it under rule 25. So read at EZK.43.19, EZK.43.23 and EZK.43.25. The competing reading marks בָּקָר unrepresented beside *young*, but no morpheme owns a part of the one English word.

The pronominal suffix of אֲדֹנָי in the formula אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה is `unrepresented`: the ASV writes *the Lord Jehovah* with no possessive, the supplied *the* belonging to אֲדֹנָי under rule 15. So read at EZK.43.18, EZK.43.19 and EZK.43.27. BSB represents this suffix and disagrees at all three.

דֶּרֶךְ הַקָּדִים is read twice over in this chapter and the ASV licenses both. Where the ASV spends its one English word on the preposition — *toward the east* at EZK.43.1, *is toward the east* at EZK.43.4 — rule 19's rider gives that word to the construct and the article takes the written *the*. Where the ASV writes a noun for דֶּרֶךְ as well — *the way of the east* at EZK.43.2, *by the way of the gate* at EZK.43.4 — rule 19's first sentence stands and the *of* goes to the rectum. Decide it by rule 19's subtraction test, not by the phrase.

report: Checked all 59 candidate lemma groups, and read the dump end to end for `added` units, which the table cannot see. One real cross-verse split, in one verse; one contract gap, amended.

SPLIT: the construction-supplied copula in a verbless clause with a prepositional predicate. EZK.43.2 (כְּ to *was like*), EZK.43.3 (כְ to *it was according to*; כַּ to *were like*) and EZK.43.19 (מִ to *are of*) all put it on the preposition heading the predicate, per rule 49. EZK.43.8 alone put *there was* on the subject noun קִיר and left בֵּין holding only *between*. Nothing in the source licenses the difference: rule 49 states the ordinary copular case is settled and that the corpus never moves the copula onto the noun instead, and rule 20's presentative sentence puts the dummy *there* on whichever unit bears that copula, expressly including a prepositional predicate. EZK.43.8 patched; no other verse touched.

NOT splits, with reasons. דֶּרֶךְ (43.1/43.2/43.4) is rule 19's rider where the ASV spends its one word on the preposition, and rule 19's first sentence where דֶּרֶךְ keeps an English noun of its own. אֵת taking *to*/*unto*/*for* (43.10, 43.11, 43.26) against the verb taking a supplied preposition (43.19, 43.20) is rule 44's stated limit — a marker stands on the object in the first set and not in the second. A supplied object *it* is `added` where no object morpheme stands (43.11, 43.22, 43.23) and carried by a suffix where one does (43.20, 43.21, 43.26). בֶּן־בָּקָר fuses to *young* identically in 43.19, 43.23 and 43.25. The waw and article buckets are ASV-driven throughout, including the unrepresented waws of 43.13 and 43.19, where the ASV writes no connective at all.

BSB: no genuine error among the 25 disagreements. The 11 Td and 4 To items are the documented convention difference. שָׁם (43.7) is rule 22 — the ASV's *where* is written for אֲשֶׁר, and the two are held apart by the verb, so rule 30's contiguity condition blocks a fusion. הֵם (43.19) is rule 20: the relative takes *that*, the copula goes to the prepositional predicate, and the pronoun has nothing left. אֶחָד (43.13), the לְ of 43.17 and the three אֲדֹנָי suffixes are places the ASV writes no word at all. סָבִיב (43.12) is the doubled occurrence rendered once. No accepted edge was changed to improve the aggregate.

AMENDMENT to rule 52. Its closing sentence gives a construct-licensed *when* to the nomen rectum only 'where none [no preposition] is present'. EZK.43.18's בְּיוֹם הֵעָשׂוֹתוֹ to *in the day when they shall make it* has a preposition present that has already spent its English on *in*, so the literal rule would force a second word onto it against rule 2. The rule already reasons this way for עֵת הִדְרִיכָהּ; the amendment widens the condition to a preposition whose own word is already written, and cites rule 42's counting. בְּיוֹם plus infinitive recurs across the OT, so the gap would otherwise be paid for by every later chapter.

One thing left standing that a later reader may want: EZK.43.25 gives *every* to the distributive לְ of לַיּוֹם and marks the assimilated article unrepresented, naming the competing rule 41 reading in its note. The corpus does record 7 units aligning הַ to *every*, including bracketed forms. It is a single occurrence, not a chapter-internal split, and the note is what rule 8 asks for, so I left the edge alone.
